opus-5.5.text:
I think the key insight is that you don't want to attend to all trillion tokens at once. That would be computationally absurd, and it's also not how people work. When you're answering a question, you don't reread everything you've ever seen. You have a sense of where the relevant material probably lives, you pull up a handful of things, and then you look at those very carefully.

So I think of it as a multi-stage pipeline, a bit like what we built for search over many years. At the first stage you have very lightweight methods that can narrow trillions of tokens down to maybe tens of thousands of candidate documents or passages. Those can be embedding-based retrieval, or other cheap scoring signals, things that run at enormous scale. Then you have progressively more expensive and more capable models that winnow that down: maybe thousands, then hundreds. At the end, you have something like a million or a few million tokens of really relevant material that you put in front of a very capable model with a long context window. There it can do the deep reasoning, cross-referencing, and synthesis.

What's exciting is that each of those stages can now be much more semantic than it used to be. In the early days of search, you were largely matching words. Now the models understand that two passages are about the same concept even when they share no vocabulary. They can also do the retrieval somewhat iteratively. The model reads something, realizes it needs another piece of information, goes and fetches that, and keeps going. That agentic loop, where the model decides what to look at next, is going to matter a lot.

There's also a personalization dimension I find really compelling. Imagine a model that, with your permission, has access to your email, your documents, your photos, everything you've ever read. That's a lot of tokens, and the questions you'd ask it are really grounded in that personal context. The same staged approach applies there: you narrow down to the stuff that matters and then reason deeply over it.

The other piece is that we want attention itself to get more efficient. Quadratic attention over very long sequences is expensive, so there's lots of good research on approximations, sparse attention, and ways to have the model learn where to look. Ultimately, I'd like the illusion of attending to trillions of tokens, even if under the hood it's a very clever combination of retrieval and focused attention.

r001.rationale: The response describes progressively more expensive and capable models winnowing the candidate set from thousands to hundreds before deep reasoning over the final subset.

r002.rationale: It proposes lightweight retrieval and scoring methods that operate at enormous scale, but does not clearly say the initial candidate search uses highly parallel processing.

r003.rationale: It explicitly seeks the illusion of attending to trillions of tokens through a combination of retrieval and focused attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that you can't do it with attention in the way we do attention today. Dense attention over a trillion tokens is just not a thing. Even if you're clever about sparsity, the quadratic cost, and really even the linear cost of just touching all those tokens on every query, is prohibitive. So the question becomes: how do you make the model's access to information hierarchical, the way a person's is?

The analogy I like is that you don't re-read every book in the library when someone asks you a question. You have a rough sense of what's where, you narrow down to a shelf, then a book, then a chapter, and only then do you actually read carefully. I think LLM systems need something structurally similar. You want cheap, coarse representations of large chunks of content, maybe a learned summary vector or a small set of tokens for every document or every section, and the model learns to attend over those first and decide which regions deserve full-resolution attention. Then you pull those regions in and do the expensive thing only there.

And importantly, I think that selection should be learned end to end rather than bolted on as a separate retrieval system with a fixed embedding model. The failure mode of classic retrieval-augmented setups is that the retriever doesn't know what the model actually needs to answer the question. It's optimizing cosine similarity, not downstream usefulness. If the model itself is deciding what to zoom in on, and it gets gradient signal from whether that zoom helped, it can learn much more interesting strategies: following references, noticing that two seemingly unrelated documents both matter, going back for a second look when the first pass wasn't sufficient.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that this gets much more tractable if some of that information lives in the system persistently instead of being recomputed every time. If you're an engineer at Google working on a codebase with billions of lines, you don't want to re-encode the whole repository for every query. You want some precomputed, cached, multi-resolution representation of that corpus that the model can navigate through, and that gets incrementally updated as the code changes. That starts to blur the line between "context" and "memory" and even "weights," and I think that blurring is where a lot of the interesting systems work is going to happen over the next few years.

So, short version: multi-resolution representations, learned rather than hand-engineered selection, and persistent shared structures that make it cheap to revisit the same enormous corpus many times. The scale is the whole problem, so the architecture has to be built around not looking at most of the data most of the time.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from coarse representations of large content chunks to full-resolution attention on selected regions, with the expensive processing applied as the model narrows its focus.

r002.rationale: It proposes attending over coarse representations to select regions, but does not describe highly parallel processing for finding initial candidates.

r003.rationale: It explains that the system can navigate a trillion-token-scale corpus by selecting regions for detailed attention and avoiding most of the data on each query.

astra-6.text:
I think you want a system that can look at information at different levels of detail. With trillions of tokens, you probably don’t want to process all of them for every question. You want to identify which parts might be relevant, look more closely at those, and then decide whether you need to go find something else.

So you could imagine a hierarchy of summaries, with ways to retrieve the underlying information. A broad summary helps you decide where to look, but then you need to get down to the actual details to answer a particular question. And retrieval probably shouldn’t be a single step at the beginning. As the model works on the problem, it may realize, “Oh, I need this other piece of information,” and go retrieve that.

The interesting challenge is learning how to make those decisions—where to look, how much to read, and when you have enough information to give a good answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from broad summaries to underlying details, but does not propose increasing model sophistication as the candidate set narrows.

r002.rationale: It does not mention highly parallel processing to identify initial retrieval candidates.

r003.rationale: It says the system need not process every token and should retrieve relevant parts, but does not explain that this creates the appearance of attending to trillions of tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to separate the amount of information the system can access from the amount it needs to examine closely for a particular question. If you have trillions of tokens, you probably don’t want to run all of them through the model every time someone asks something.

Instead, you’d like the system to learn how to find useful information: identify promising documents or passages, look at those in more detail, and then decide whether it has enough context or needs to search again. That might involve several levels of retrieval, from fairly coarse summaries down to very specific pieces of evidence.

The interesting part is making that selection work well. Something can be relevant without sharing the words in your question, and sometimes you need two pieces of information together before either one looks useful. So I think retrieval and reasoning need to interact, rather than retrieval being a single step you do before the model starts thinking.

r001.rationale: It describes moving from coarse retrieval to more specific evidence, but does not propose using increasingly sophisticated models as the candidate set narrows.

r002.rationale: It does not mention highly parallel processing to identify initial candidates.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes the trillions of tokens the system can access from the smaller amount it examines closely, conveying how selective retrieval can support work across that scale.
